The Cardinal snapper Pristipomoides macrophthalmus is a deep-water lutjanid distributed across the Indo-Pacific region, where it inhabits rocky slopes and drop-offs at depths between 100 and 300 meters. The emerging yolk-sac larvae are minute, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.00029 grams [Wwb = just 0.00029 grams], reflecting the small egg diameter of 0.82 millimeters from which they hatch. This minimal initial mass necessitates a rapid transition to exogenous feeding during the pelagic larval phase.

Field collections have shown that gravid females with developing oocytes are encountered throughout much of the year, suggesting a protracted spawning season in this tropical species.

At the ambient temperature of 18.4 °C [T = 18.4 °C], the daily reproduction rate inferred from comparative analyses corresponds to approximately 931 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 931 eggs per day], derived from an annual fecundity of approximately 340,000 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 340,000 eggs per year]. This high fecundity is characteristic of many deep-water lutjanids and compensates for the relatively low survival rates experienced during the prolonged pelagic larval stage.
